cognate: Ved. vácas- = Gk ἔπος (*wékʷos, neuter s-stem, exact); Ved. √śru- (śr̥ṇavat, śr̥ṇotu) = Gk κλύω (ἔκλυες, Il. 16.236/14.234) (*ḱlew-); 1sg possessor (Ved. gen. me / Gk ἐμόν, ἐμάν)
drift_or_renewal: In Pindar the verb is renewed as ἀκούω (ἀρὰν ἄκουσας) inside a line that keeps ἔπος and the address to the Father; Homer keeps the cognate verb (ἐμὸν ἔπος ἔκλυες). Possessor: Vedic enclitic genitive me vs Greek possessive adjective.
shared_syntax: verb 'hear' + object 'word(s)' of the speaking worshipper, addressed to a god: Ved. (deity) śr̥ṇavat vácāṃsi me 'may he hear my words' ~ Gk ποτ' ἐμὸν ἔπος ἔκλυες 'once you heard my word'
context: Prayer formula asking a god to hear the poet's words. RV 10.66.11c and RV 10.64.10a-b are Viśvedeva prayers ('may Ahi Budhnya hear my words', 'may the Mother hear us, Tvaṣṭar the father ... the word'). Il. 16.236 is Achilles' prayer to Zeus (and Il. 14.234 Hera's plea to Hypnos), and Pindar I. 6.42 is Heracles' prayer to Father Zeus, which takes up the Homeric line ('if ever, Father Zeus, you heard my prayer'). The Vedic stanza names a pitā́ alongside the prayer to hear vácaḥ, and the Pindar line has Ζεῦ πάτερ beside ἔπος. Both traditions use their high-register word for 'utterance' (vácas, ἔπος), not the ordinary word, and both use it in the same construction. This matches the established Ved. śrudhí ~ Gk κλῦθι prayer opening. Avestan vacə̄ srūidiiāi (Y 45.5) shows the same collocation in Iranian.

cognate: Gk εὐρεῖα = Ved. urvī́ (fem. of urú-, *h₁urHéwih₂ < *h₁wérHus); Gk χθών = Ved. kṣám- = Av. zam- (*dʰéǵʰōm); Ved. pṛthivī́ = Av. pərəθβī (*pl̥th₂éwih₂ 'the broad one', root *pleth₂-)
drift_or_renewal: Indo-Iranian lexicalized the epithet *pl̥th₂éwih₂ 'broad' as the name of Earth (Ved. pṛthivī́). Vedic then adds urvī́ to pṛthivī́/bhū́mi-, keeping *dʰéǵʰōm + urvī́ only in RV 6.17.7a (kṣā́m ... urvī́m). Avestan keeps zam- with the *pleth₂- epithet (ząm pərəθβīm paθanąm). Greek keeps χθών with the *h₁wérHus epithet (εὐρεῖα χθών).
shared_syntax: attributive epithet 'wide/broad' + noun 'earth' (fem. adjective agreeing with the earth-noun)
context: Cosmic Earth as 'the wide/broad one'. Hesiod Sc. 373 (and Il. 21.387, which follows slab passage Il. 21.386) has the wide earth resounding under charging horses or colliding gods. AVŚ 11.2.19 lists Rudra's realms, 'yours are the quarters, heaven, earth (pṛthivī), this wide (uru) atmosphere'. RV 10.170.3d urú paprathe 'has spread wide' puts both roots of the formula, *h₁wérHu- and *pleth₂-, in one verbal phrase. 'Broad' is not the obvious epithet for earth: Homer could say μέλαινα, πουλυβότειρα, ζείδωρος; Vedic could say mahī́, dhruvā. The *h₁wérHu-/*pleth₂- pair recurs in all three branches (RV 6.17.7a kṣā́m ... urvī́m is the exact Greek match in Vedic; Av. Y 10.4 ząm pərəθβīm paθanąm). That argues for an inherited epithet of Earth rather than independent description. The slab anchors carry the epithet roots next to the earth-word but not as a fused phrase in Indic, which keeps this at medium.

cognate: Ved. āśú- = Gk ὠκύς (*h₁ōḱú-); Ved. áśva- = Gk ἵππος (*h₁éḱwos), the noun appearing in Greek only in support passages
drift_or_renewal: none in the core formula. In the Greek slab anchor the epithet sits with another noun (βέλος ὠκύ 'swift missile'), and the horse formula ὠκέες ἵπποι is in support only. In RV 10.68.2d āśú- is used substantivally for racehorses ('like swift ones at the race').
shared_syntax: epithet + noun, adjective agreeing with the noun 'horse' (Ved. áśvam ... āśúm, acc. sg.; Gk ὠκέας ἵππους). Vedic and Greek both allow the adjective to stand for the noun (āśávaḥ / ὠκέες as racers).
context: Horses praised for speed in racing and chariot contexts. RV 10.107.10a: they groom the swift horse for the generous patron. RV 10.68.2d: like swift (horses) at the race. Homer has ὠκέες ἵπποι of chariot teams. The Greek slab anchor shows ὠκύς as a fixed epic epithet (βέλος ὠκύ, a recurring hemistich). The exact horse formula, though, is in support (35 Homeric lines) and is the well-known *h₁éḱwōs h₁ōḱéwes equation, with Av. āsu.aspa- as a third witness from memory. Recalled from the literature. The anchoring in this slab is partial.

cognate: Ved. uṣás- = Gk ἠώς (*h₂éwsōs). Ved. devī́ (*deyw-ih₂) and Gk δῖα (*diw-yə, fem. of δῖος = Ved. divyá-) both come from *dyew- 'sky, divine' but with different suffixes.
drift_or_renewal: The epithet is built on the same root with different derivatives (devī́ vs δῖα). In the slab anchor itself devī́ is the coming Night (nominative), set beside uṣásam rather than agreeing with it. The fused epithet uṣā́ḥ devī́ / úṣo devi is in support.
shared_syntax: Dawn-goddess name + feminine *dyew-derived epithet 'divine/heavenly' (Ved. uṣā́ḥ devī́, voc. úṣo devi; Gk acc. Ἠῶ δῖαν)
context: Night giving way to Dawn. RV 10.127 is the Night hymn: the goddess Night, coming, has pushed out her sister Dawn (3a-b). Il. 18.255: not to wait on the plain for divine Dawn. The Odyssey formula ἐμείναμεν Ἠῶ δῖαν is likewise about waiting through the night until divine Dawn. The *dyew-epithet fits Dawn as 'daughter of the sky' (Ved. divó duhitā́). Against this, δῖος and devī́ are both very common generic epithets, so chance agreement is a real possibility. Low.

cognate: Gk μέθυ = Ved. mádhu- (*médʰu); Gk ἡδύς = Ved. svādú- (*swéh₂dus)
drift_or_renewal: Greek μέθυ has drifted from 'honey/mead' to 'wine'. Vedic mádhu keeps 'honey, sweet drink (soma)'.
shared_syntax: noun 'mead' + attributive 'sweet' (Gk μέθυ ἡδύ; Ved. svā́do ... mádho, mádhu svā́dma, mádhvaḥ svā́diṣṭham)
context: Food and drink offered or consumed. Od. 7.265: Calypso provisions Odysseus with σῖτον καὶ μέθυ ἡδύ. RV 1.187.2a addresses Food (pitú-) as 'sweet food, honeyed food', the same food + sweet + mádhu nexus. The Vedic slab anchor (RV 10.123.3d, licking the mádhu of the immortal) has the noun but not the adjective, so the anchoring is thin. The pairing could also arise naturally from 'honey is sweet'. Low.

note: All 147 bundles read. Claims: hear-my-word prayer formula, broad earth, swift horses (medium); Dawn divine, sweet mead (low). Leads rejected as generic or chance: fat cattle (B-36980), licking amṛta/ambrosia (B-37089: Aristophanic comic use), stan- 'thunder/groan' + cloud (B-449cf), winter/spring merism (B-a6dfa), foam phéna/spūma (B-cbe11), 'put fear in heart' with *dʰeh₁- (B-f1a63), tongue+voice (B-c8988).
